1de13f6f28c972b9dda1ab35f09238a7.text: In the wake of the Bald Range wildfire, an international study is seeking volunteers from the South Okanagan for a new treatment method for those dealing with post-traumatic stress disorder. Penticton in the South Okanagan is one of four B.C. communities, alongside Kelowna, Kamloops and North Vancouver, selected to participate in the study. The impacts of the Bald Range wildfire, which saw thousands of people forced out of their homes in the Okanagan, left behind more than physical scars on the region. About 150 structures, including homes and accessory structures, were destroyed within the Regional District of Okanagan Similkameen and District of Summerland as a result of the fast-moving Aug. 7 blaze. Faulder was particularly hard hit by the fire, as the closest community to the origin point. The cause of the fire remains under investigation. “PTSD touches so many people in our community: first responders, people who’ve survived accidents or violence, families who lost homes to fire. Being part of rigorous, closely supervised research means people in the South Okanagan have a real voice in what the next generation of care looks like,” said Dr. Linda Grasswick, principal investigator for the study in Penticton. Medical Arts Health Research Group is conducting the study under Health Canada and research ethics oversight. The treatment will explore an investigational form of psilocybin, one of the naturally occurring compounds found in many so-called “magic” mushrooms. Adults living with PTSD in the South Okanagan who would like to learn more can contact the study team confidentially at (888) 490-4320 or visit www.healthresearch.ca. Reaching out does not commit anyone to participate. Those interested will be screened by a doctor to determine whether the study is a safe and appropriate fit. Participants will receive care and support from a dedicated study team throughout, and study-related visits, assessments, and the investigational medication are provided at no cost.

Courtney McCowan's family is seeking answers after she died outside of Port Hardy Hospital on Nov. 19. The family of a 48-year-old woman who died outside Port Hardy Hospital on Nov. 19 is seeking answers. Her friend tried to get her into (the) emergency (department). They denied her. They wouldn’t let her in.” Schubert said a paramedic was in the parking lot cleaning an ambulance and noticed what was happening: “So, he came over to attend to my mom, and started doing CPR. They had called 911, so then two other ambulances from a nearby ambulance station came over to help.” According to Schubert, at this point, no one from the hospital was letting them in. “At that point, 39 minutes later, for whatever reason, they changed their minds and they decided to let her in, but by that point it was too late.” In a statement, B.C. Minister of Health Ryan Peterson said, “Our thoughts are with the family members and loved ones impacted by the tragic outcome that happened on the grounds of the Port Hardy Hospital on Thursday (Nov. 19).” The Ministry noted that Island Health and BC Emergency Health Services are investigating the circumstances of this incident. “What we know at this time is that both Island Health care providers and BCEHS paramedics responded and provided emergency interventions,” Peterson added. “Access to health care is one of our government’s top priorities. 980e89f1cefd532da0a68ec27e65a18c.text: Visitors to Barkerville during its Olde-Fashioned Christmas weekend can experience traditional sleigh rides through the historic site. Anyone looking for a very special Christmas adventure, as well as a trip back in time, can experience both during Barkerville Historic Town & Park’s Olde-Fashioned Christmas, which takes place from Dec. 11–13. The celebration allows visitors to enjoy the sights and sounds of Christmas past in one of British Columbia’s most iconic historic settings: Barkerville. Located approximately 80 kilometres east of Quesnel, the town was born when Billy Barker struck gold on Williams Creek in 1862. Today, the National Historic Site brings the Gold Rush era to life through more than 125 heritage buildings, exhibits, demonstrations, and costumed performers in a spectacular setting. Barkerville’s Olde-Fashioned Christmas festivities begin on Friday, Dec. 11, when visitors can enjoy a selection of activities, demonstrations, and shopping ahead of the weekend celebration. While not all businesses and activities will be operating on Friday, a variety of shops, exhibits, and programs will be available, allowing people to explore and enjoy the unique atmosphere of Barkerville in winter. Throughout Saturday and Sunday, visitors can enjoy carolling, guided town tours, traditional school lessons, demonstrations at the blacksmith shop and print shop, and Christmas shopping while exploring many of the town’s historic buildings and exhibits. Programming will also include Indigenous interpretation at the Kelly Hall and a holiday reading with Chartres Brew, B.C.’s first chief inspector of police who also served as gold commissioner and judge. The Correlieu Concert Band will be returning to join in the merriment on Sunday, Dec. 13. Returning favourites will also include horse-drawn sleigh rides through the historic townsite, and this year visitors will have the opportunity to book special evening sleigh rides and experience Barkerville as Christmas lights

fe57c81843c463633b34e743f7cedfcc.text: Quesnel U11 Blue Devils bring home silver from Clearwater tournament. The Quesnel U11 Blue Devils battled their way to a silver-medal finish at a 10-team tournament in Clearwater from Dec. 13-15. In an email to the *Observer,* head coach Brett Roberts said the Blue Devils opened the tournament with a pair of hard-fought victories, defeating West Kelowna 4-2 and North Okanagan 7-5. The team followed that up with a dominant 10-0 win over host Clearwater to secure second place in the round-robin standings. On Sunday morning, Quesnel faced third-place Kamloops in the semifinals, with a spot in the gold-medal game against Langley on the line. Roberts said the Blue Devils came out of the gates quickly with a 3-0 lead over Kamloops after the first period. The second period saw the Quesnel team take a 6-0 lead into the third, but penalties started to pile on late in the middle frame, resulting in a slow start to the third. Kamloops popped three quick goals to start the third and draw within three, but the Blue Devils expanded their lead to 7-3 shortly after, enough to advance to the finals. Roberts added that the Blue Devils took on a 13-man Langley squad in the finals, with just eight skaters and a goalie. Langley’s speed and team play proved difficult to contain, as the team opened the scoring five minutes into the first period and went on to claim a 6-1 victory. “More important than a silver medal on the ice is the fact that this tournament brought us closer together off the ice,” Roberts said. “When you see kids gelling at the hotel or at team dinner, those are the intangibles that turn us from hockey players into a hockey team.” Roberts also praised the team’s effort throughout the weekend, pointing to the work ethic that helped the Blue Devils reach the championship game. “As a coaching staff, we couldn’t be more proud of the work ethic that we displayed over the weekend. When you think of Quesnel, you think blue-collar and that’s exactly what got us to the finals,”

3cc11baa70f11b295e3395ae72d3f6fa.text: WL Kitty Spay founder Cassidy Porter and vice president Crystal Sheridan were at Cariboo Corner on Saturday, Nov. 21 for their first annual Pet Vendor Market. Collecting donations in Williams Lake to assist feline owners cover the costs for spaying and neutering is how Cassidy Porter helps the furry animals she is severely allergic to. It has just been over two years since Porter founded the non-profit WL Kitty Spay that hosted its first Pet Vendor Market on Saturday, Nov. 21 at Cariboo Corner. Wearing a holiday cat themed pullover sweater Porter was joined with vice president Crystal Sheridan at the afternoon event where people could purchase entries for one of three Christmas baskets and learn more about WL Kitty Spay. Also available were pet dishes donated by Save-On-Foods and harnesses and collars provided by pet stores in the Lower Mainland. “We just wanted a chance to raise money for our spay and neuter program, and thought we would try something different and tailor it to pet themed items for the the public,” Porter said of the Pet Market that coincided with several holiday craft markets. Since launching WL Kitty Spay, more than 170 cats have been spayed or neutered through providing financial support for the costs of the procedure in addition to a microchip and cone collar. With 30 cats on their waitlist and donations having slowed down for a bit, Porter said they had to currently suspend any additions to the list. She is hopeful, however, with the holiday season that donations will increase and they’ll be able to open up their waitlist again in the New Year. “Even with a double income household, times are tough right now and everything is really expensive,” she added. “It’ s expensive to fix your animals, and the cat overpopulation is pretty extreme right now so we just want to do what we can to help.” In a November 2026 news release, the BC SPCA stated pet overpopulation has been an increasing concern across the province, especially where cats may roam

8f5ac0698ce9cbc0be75a679a3f65d1b.text: Stephanie Higginson has been elected MLA for Ladysmith Oceanside following a judicial recount of the vote. Stephanie Higginson has finally been confirmed as MLA for Ladysmith Oceanside, following a judicial recount. The final results for the electoral district totalled 14,352 for Higginson of the BC NDP (44.4 per cent of the vote), narrowly defeating Kris McNichol of the Conservative Party, who garnered 14,305 votes, or 44.25 per cent of the vote, according to Elections BC. Charlene Smylie of the BC Green Party had 3,617 votes, or 11.19 per cent. There were 51 “rejected ballots”, according to Elections BC. “It felt really good to know that we’d come to an end and the riding and the constituency had officially elected me. It comes with a lot of responsibility and also a big honour. I’m just really thrilled to be back in the position,” Higginson said. Higginson and McNichol went into the judicial recount just 13 votes apart, which widened to 47 when the recount concluded. “Congratulations to Stephanie. She ran a good campaign. I thought we ran a good campaign. Smylie ran a good campaign,” McNichol said, and noted the riding totalled the most votes in B.C. in the provincial election. “We made some inroads, obviously, and when you look at all of British Columbia, they spoke. They wanted change. Apparently Ladysmith Oceanside didn’t want the change needed, but we sure gave it a run.” He added that nothing will change for him, as a businessman, and he is back to running his businesses, rather than heading to Victoria. “We move forward. It was a long road to get here,” McNichol said, and added he is grateful to his volunteers, supporters and campaign team: “They’re the ones I’m doing this for”. Higginson said that during the month-long process, she tried to keep things in perspective, recognizing that she would have her family and her health, regardless of the final election outcome. “The uncertainty of how you’re going to be spending your time, it was getting a bit long

Two black bear cubs have been struck and killed by a vehicle along the Trans-Canada Highway near Goldstream Park. The BC Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) confirmed they received a report Monday morning (Nov. 23). “Conservation officers responded to assess and address any immediate public safety concerns along this busy stretch of highway,” said a BCCOS statement. “Two cubs were located deceased.” Emcon Services, the contractor responsible for provincial highway maintenance, confirmed they were called to collect the two bears. A spokesperson said the carcasses were “disposed of appropriately.” Sooke-based wildlife organization Wild Wise said it was “devastated” to hear of the incident. They said the death of the two cubs serves as a reminder of how important it is to remain vigilant when driving through areas where wildlife may be present. “Please slow down, watch for wildlife near roadways, and be especially attentive during periods of low visibility,” they said in a social media post. To avoid bear-vehicle collisions, the Wildlife Collision Prevention Program – which aims to make B.C.’s highways safer for both people and wildlife through education and awareness – drivers should drive defensively, concentrating on the road at all times. Drivers should watch the sides of the road for wildlife attempting to cross, especially where visibility is poor, using extra caution at night. In the event of a collision, the organization advises drivers to always call BCCOS on 1-877-952-7277 if there is an injured animal to report. “A wounded animal can be very dangerous,” they say. “You are not required to put an injured animal out of its misery.” If there is damage over $1,000, any human injuries, or the animal carcass is not safe to be moved and presents an urgent highway safety issue, WCPP says to call the RCMP. Nanaimo community members and allies solemnly packed Sands Funeral Chapel on Friday, mourning the lives lost over the past year on Transgender Day of Remembrance. Transgender Day of Remembrance began in 1999 to remember the lives of transgender people whose lives were taken to anti-trans violence. A total of 373 names were recognized this year who died from suicide or violence, in addition to two names from cancer and one from HIV. Five names come from Canada, including two from Vancouver. During the Nanaimo vigil held on Nov. 20, Nathan Rokeby, a transgender 15-year-old boy, read a poem in one of the past victim’s memory. He stated that as a trans youth, he fears each election as some provincial governments institute laws targeting trans people. “I can’t be expected to be unaffected as I watch adults I’m supposed to look up to create laws with the intent to silence me and the result to kill me. I am trans, I am proud of it, but I am also a kid. I am the boy who wishes I could have a say, I am the child who wants to grow up,” he said. “Let me love, let me live, let me grow up like so many of us didn’t.” Lauren Semple, president of the Nanaimo Pride Society, said that while over 300 names were recorded this year, she knows with “devastating certainty” that the numbers are likely higher, but the victims were denied their trans identity in death. “We are living through a time of unprecedented legislative and physical hostility,” she said. Semple cited the number of bills targeting trans people in the United States alone, which, according to Trans Legislation Tracker, totalled 1,022 bills in 2025, 126 passing. “The global impact is equally staggering. 305e2b4d9181ca6636a308a783cdb43a.text: A police laser reading showing a blue BMW that was allegedly going 208 km/h in a 90 zone on B.C.'s Sea to Sky Highway. A 22-year-old California man was allegedly caught going 118 kilometres an hour over the posted speed limit on the Sea to Sky Highway. A B.C. Highway Patrol officer saw a southbound blue BMW driving “much faster” than other traffic on Highway 99 near Squamish on Nov. 1 around 5:10 p.m., according to a news release from police on Tuesday (Nov. 24). The officer used his police laser and got a speed reading of 208 km/h in a 90 zone, the release says. “Even by the standards of the Sea to Sky Highway, this is a terribly dangerous speed,” Sgt. Michael McLaughlin said. “Visitors to B.C. are expected to understand and obey our traffic laws. You will not ‘get a break’ just to avoid the inconvenience of losing your vehicle and interrupting your vacation plans.” The driver was issued a $483-fine for excessive speed over 60 km/h, as well as the cost of a tow truck and a seven-day impound. “No matter whether it’s locals or visitors, treating the Sea to Sky like the autobahn has got to stop. There is a direct correlation between dangerous driving and deadly collisions that shut this highway down for hours at a time,” McLaughlin said.

ce583d7cfa9388385315ff51e949dc3a.text: Conservative candidate Kristina Loewen won the Kelowna Centre riding by 132 votes on election night, Oct. 24, 2026. Conservative Party of BC candidate Kristina Loewen has won Kelowna Centre following a judicial recount, widening her margin over the BC NDP’s Loyal Wooldridge, to 46 votes. In a Facebook post, Loewen announced that the recount was complete. Elections BC posted the results on its website Tuesday (Nov. 23) afternoon, confirming the totals. “The Kelowna Centre recount is done!!! I’ve now won with a margin of 46 votes (up from 43)!!!!” Loewen wrote on Facebook. “I’m ready to be able to fully move forward in my role as an MLA representing Kelowna Centre – as well as in my new role as Minister of Children and Family Development.” Loewen also thanked Wooldridge and OneBC candidate Bill Desrossier for contesting the seat. Following election night on Oct. 24, Loewen held a lead of 132 to 137 votes over Wooldridge before mail-in, absentee, and telephone ballots were counted during Elections BC’s final count between Nov. 6-8. Once those ballots were factored in, Loewen’s advantage narrowed to 43 votes—11,689 votes to Wooldridge’s 11,646 votes. Because the margin fell below Election BC’s automatic judicial recount threshold of one-500th of total ballots cast (48 votes in Kelowna Centre), the riding headed back to a judicial recount which started Nov. 23. The finish echoed the 2024 provincial election where Loewen and Wooldridge also battled down to the wire, and a judicial recount was also needed.

Tumbler Ridge shooting alleged co-conspirator, James Cody Bryant, pleaded not guilty and will face a now-delayed trial there in December, 2027. The accused co-conspirator in the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting is requesting to be released from custody as her counsel argues she doesn’t pose a risk to the community. It comes as the previously scheduled trial that was set to begin next month is pushed back a year. Melody Bryant’s counsel filed the request in the Western District of Washington U.S. District Court in Seattle on Nov. 18. Bryant was denied bail by Judge Mary Alice Theiler on Oct. 13. Bryant was charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country on Oct. 6 as James Cody Bryant, but uses the name Melody and pronouns she and her as she is transgender. The latest court filings refer to her as Ms. Bryant. The filing says that Bryant was interviewed by investigators two days after the killings and she “cooperated fully and cried throughout the interview, expressing horror and disbelief at (shooter Jesse) Van Rootselaar’s crimes.” There was a second voluntary interview on March 3 after reviewing a complete copy of the Discord chat between Bryant and Van Rootselaar. “After that second interview, for seven months, investigators left Ms. Bryant in the community without any restrictions on her movement or access to the internet,” the filing argues. Counsel says that Bryant has a stable residence, no criminal history, employment history and “strong community ties.” The document notes that U.S. Probation has reviewed her housing and community ties and found that both favour her release. The filing adds that there is “no evidence” that Bryant has ever been in contact with another person with similarly violent fantasies or that she visits sites or chat communities that glorify violence. 1342e4a0399b40a9728a00b9f6f640b5.text: Photo of weapons seized from the last 2 months of pro-active enforcement in Prince George, British Columbia. The Prince George RCMP has seized a significant cache of weapons during ongoing proactive enforcement efforts targeting public safety concerns in the downtown core. According to an RCMP press release, the seizures were carried out by the RCMP’s Problem Oriented Policing (POP) Unit and Downtown Safety Unit (DSU) as part of targeted initiatives addressing crime and disorder. Mounties said among the items seized was a large assortment of edged and improvised weapons, pellet and replica-style firearms, batons, brass knuckles and a crossbow with bolts. “The work of our Problem Oriented Policing and Downtown Safety teams continues to have a direct impact on community safety,” Sgt. Craig Douglass of the Prince George RCMP said. “The removal of these weapons reduces the potential for violence and demonstrates our commitment to proactive policing in areas where residents and businesses have identified safety concerns.” Police said the seizures are the result of ongoing collaboration between specialized enforcement teams focused on repeat offenders, weapon possession and crime trends affecting the downtown area. The Prince George RCMP said it remains committed to working with community partners to improve public safety and maintain a safe environment for residents, visitors and businesses.
